title: Ice Cream 1.5L

drivers.name: TikTok trend
drivers.evidence: No prior data on TikTok trends, but past promotions (noise-adjusted x1.25) suggest potential lift. This is a new driver; shrink toward 1.0 due to low evidence count.

drivers.name: Price increase
drivers.evidence: 2.3% price hike from 6.41 to 6.56. Past data shows no strong price sensitivity, but price increases typically reduce demand. Applied conservative downside.

adjustment.analysis: Baseline median is 44.6. Halloween has a negligible historical lift (noise-adjusted x1.0). Price increased 2.3% from 6.41 to 6.56—price hikes typically reduce demand, but this is modest. The product is trending on TikTok, a novel driver with no prior data. Past promotions lifted sales by 57% median, but noise-adjusted to x1.25; this is a new, untested trend. Given the lack of prior evidence for viral trends, shrink effect toward 1.0. The classical model suggests no uplift, but TikTok is a strong signal. Adjust up moderately, with high uncertainty.

KNOWN PLAN FOR THE TARGET WEEK:
  events: Holiday: Halloween (Sat)
  shelf price: 6.56 (+2.3% vs regular price 6.41)
  planner notes: Product is trending on TikTok

STATISTICAL BASELINE (exponential smoothing of recent sales; it ignores events, promotions and prices):
  median 44.6 | 5%-95%: 17.1 - 70.6 | 10%-90%: 24.4 - 66.9

In the evidence below, 'vs baseline' = actual units / what this same baseline predicted for that week.
It is the multiplier that would have been right, so it maps directly onto median_multiplier.
This product's ordinary weeks already swing about +/-36% around the baseline, so a past effect smaller than that, seen only a few times, is mostly noise. The
'noise-adjusted estimate' is the effect shrunk toward x1.0 for that noise and the number of sightings.
